items.stem: Which term describes the view that media messages are “injected” into a passive audience and have direct, immediate effects?
items.answer: Hypodermic syringe model
items.markingKey: Hypodermic syringe model: the view that media messages are “injected” into a passive audience and have direct, immediate effects. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “imitation”, and give one example.
items.answer: Copying behaviour seen in the media. Example: children copying fighting moves from cartoons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (copying behaviour seen in the media); 1 mark for a relevant example such as children copying fighting moves from cartoons. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “copycat violence” and “sensitisation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Copycat violence: violent acts that copy events seen in the media (e.g. a crime that copies a scene in a film). Sensitisation: the idea that media violence can make audiences more aware of the harm violence causes (e.g. a war film making viewers more opposed to war).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A researcher in Lima shows one group of children a violent cartoon and another a calm cartoon, then observes how they play with toys for 20 minutes. Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Interactionism: audiences interpret media actively; effects depend on meanings and context, and moral panics exaggerate media effects (Gauntlett).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Cairo shows one group of children a violent cartoon and another a calm cartoon, then observes how they play with toys for 20 minutes. Explain how an interactionist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: audiences interpret media actively; effects depend on meanings and context, and moral panics exaggerate media effects (Gauntlett).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: After two teenagers in Doha are convicted of an assault, newspapers claim they were copying a violent video game, and politicians call for the game to be banned. Explain how postmodernist and interactionist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: audiences are media-literate and fragmented; there is no single effect, as people use media in many ways. Interactionism: audiences interpret media actively; effects depend on meanings and context, and moral panics exaggerate media effects (Gauntlett).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Jonas is planning a study of the effects of violent video games on children. Evaluate the use of case studies for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they can be used to generate hypotheses that are tested later on larger samples; they may use several methods, increasing validity. Limitations: one case may be untypical, so findings cannot be generalised; the detailed data is difficult to compare with other cases. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of violent video games on children but best combined with another method such as field experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A research team is investigating the effects of violent video games on children. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: anonymity may encourage respondents to admit sensitive or embarrassing behaviour they would not reveal face to face; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of violent video games on children but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: In a laboratory experiment in Auckland, 40 children were split into two groups and observed after watching a cartoon. Table: children in each group (%) | Violent cartoon group | Non-violent cartoon group. Hit the toy at least once | 58% | 21%. Played without hitting the toy | 42% | 79%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Violent cartoon group and Non-violent cartoon group for Played without hitting the toy (Non-violent cartoon group minus Violent cartoon group)?
items.answer: +37 percentage points
items.markingKey: 79 − 42 = +37 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: In a laboratory experiment in Cairo, 40 children were split into two groups and observed after watching a cartoon. Table: children in each group (%) | Violent cartoon group | Non-violent cartoon group. Hit the toy at least once | 62% | 39%. Played without hitting the toy | 38% | 61%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Violent cartoon group and Non-violent cartoon group for Played without hitting the toy. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that media violence causes aggressive behaviour.
items.answer: (a) 61 − 38 = +23 percentage points (Non-violent cartoon group compared with Violent cartoon group). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Non-violent cartoon group than for Violent cartoon group among Played without hitting the toy; the figure is lower for Non-violent cartoon group than for Violent cartoon group among Hit the toy at least once; Played without hitting the toy had the highest figure for Non-violent cartoon group. The violent cartoon may have excited children. Qualifications: Hitting a toy is not real violence; artificial setting; short-term effect only; small sample; demand characteristics; ethical concerns. The data also come from laboratory experiments of 40 children in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 38 and 61; 1 mark for 23 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Explain two arguments that the media cause violence.
items.answer: Imitation (Bandura); desensitisation; copycat crimes; moral panics citing cases; longitudinal correlations.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Imitation (Bandura); desensitisation; copycat crimes; moral panics citing cases; longitudinal correlations. [8]

items.stem: Tomás carried out an experiment with 60 children aged 5-7, observing their play after a cartoon. Table: children in each group (%) | Violent cartoon group | Non-violent cartoon group. Hit the toy at least once | 62% | 42%. Played without hitting the toy | 38% | 58%. (a) Calculate the difference between Hit the toy at least once and Played without hitting the toy for Violent cartoon group and for Non-violent cartoon group, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of media violence and aggression. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that media violence causes aggressive behaviour.
items.answer: (a) Violent cartoon group: 24 percentage points; Non-violent cartoon group: 16 percentage points; the difference is larger for Violent cartoon group. (b) The artificial setting means people may not behave as they would in real life, so validity is low. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Non-violent cartoon group than for Violent cartoon group among Played without hitting the toy; the figure is lower for Non-violent cartoon group than for Violent cartoon group among Hit the toy at least once; Played without hitting the toy had the highest figure for Non-violent cartoon group. Children may imitate behaviour they see on screen (Bandura). Qualifications: Hitting a toy is not real violence; artificial setting; short-term effect only; small sample; demand characteristics; ethical concerns. The data also come from laboratory experiments of 60 children in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each difference (24 and 16); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Define the term “personal identity need”, and give one example.
items.answer: Using media to compare oneself with others and form one’s identity. Example: teenagers comparing themselves with characters in a drama.

items.stem: Explain the difference between “personal identity need” and “selective exposure”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Personal identity need: using media to compare oneself with others and form one’s identity (e.g. teenagers comparing themselves with characters in a drama). Selective exposure: choosing only media that fit one’s existing views and interests (e.g. reading only newspapers that support one’s party).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: During an election campaign in Doha, a respected local shopkeeper discusses the TV debates with customers, and many of them later vote the way he recommended. Suggest how a pluralist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Pluralism: audiences are active and diverse; they choose and filter media to meet their needs, so media power is limited (Blumler and McQuail, Katz and Lazarsfeld).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: During an election campaign in Dhaka, a respected local shopkeeper discusses the TV debates with customers, and many of them later vote the way he recommended. Explain how a postmodernist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: audiences use media to construct identities in a media-saturated world with endless choice.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful non-participant observation is for studying how friends influence each other’s views of news stories.
items.answer: Strengths: the researcher stays detached, so is less likely to “go native” and can record more objectively; a structured observation schedule allows behaviour to be counted and compared, improving reliability. Limitations: observation schedules impose the researcher’s categories on behaviour; the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect). Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how friends influence each other’s views of news stories but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: During an election campaign in Jakarta, a respected local shopkeeper discusses the TV debates with customers, and many of them later vote the way he recommended. Compare how pluralist and Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Pluralism: audiences are active and diverse; they choose and filter media to meet their needs, so media power is limited (Blumler and McQuail, Katz and Lazarsfeld). Marxism: audience needs are shaped by capitalist media and advertising; “choice” takes place within the limits of dominant ideology.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “drip-drip effect”? Give one example.
items.answer: The gradual influence of repeated media messages over time. Example: repeated stereotypes slowly shaping attitudes.

items.stem: Distinguish between “oppositional reading” and “preferred reading”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Oppositional reading: an interpretation that rejects the preferred reading (e.g. seeing a pro-war report as propaganda). Preferred reading: the interpretation of a text that its producers intend audiences to accept (e.g. a news report framing protesters as troublemakers).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A study in Riyadh finds that people who watch the most television news overestimate the proportion of crimes committed by young people. Suggest how a neo-Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Neo-Marxism: media texts encode a preferred, hegemonic reading, but audiences’ class positions lead to dominant, negotiated or oppositional readings (Hall).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A study in Toronto finds that people who watch the most television news overestimate the proportion of crimes committed by young people. Explain how a cultural effects sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Cultural effects theory: repeated media messages gradually shape audiences’ attitudes over time, reinforcing dominant ideas (Philo).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of field experiments for studying how different social groups interpret a TV news report.
items.answer: Strengths: they take place in a natural setting, so behaviour is more realistic than in a laboratory; one variable can be altered (for example the name on a job application) to test its effect. Limitations: they are hard to repeat exactly because conditions in the real world change; the researcher has much less control over variables than in a laboratory. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how different social groups interpret a TV news report but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Distinguish between “oppositional reading” and “negotiated reading”.
items.answer: Oppositional reading: an interpretation that rejects the preferred reading. Negotiated reading: an interpretation that accepts parts of the preferred reading but adapts it.

items.answer: Pluralism: audiences are diverse and active, so media cannot impose any single meaning on them. Interactionism: audiences actively make meanings from media in social contexts; interpretations differ by group (Morley).

items.stem: A sociologist in Mexico City wants to research the effects of violent video games on children. Evaluate the use of structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can read questions aloud, so younger or less literate respondents can take part; the interviewer can explain unclear questions, so fewer answers are spoiled. Limitations: respondents may be reluctant to reveal sensitive information face to face to a stranger following a fixed script; the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of violent video games on children but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: After two teenagers in Singapore are convicted of an assault, newspapers claim they were copying a violent video game, and politicians call for the game to be banned. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: audiences are media-literate and fragmented; there is no single effect, as people use media in many ways.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In a laboratory experiment in Kathmandu, 40 children were split into two groups and observed after watching a cartoon. Table: children in each group (%) | Violent cartoon group | Non-violent cartoon group. Hit the toy at least once | 60% | 21%. Played without hitting the toy | 40% | 79%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Violent cartoon group and Non-violent cartoon group for Hit the toy at least once (Non-violent cartoon group minus Violent cartoon group)?
items.answer: -39 percentage points
items.markingKey: 21 − 60 = -39 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Felix is planning a study of how much violence is shown on children’s television. Explain one limitation of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: They are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of how much violence is shown on children’s television. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of unstructured interviews for studying the effects of violent video games on children.
items.answer: Strengths: a sympathetic, non-judgemental interviewer can help people talk about painful or private experiences; the interviewer can follow up answers and explore meanings in the interviewee’s own words. Limitations: the power imbalance between adult researcher and child may make children say what they think adults want to hear; they are time-consuming and the data is hard to analyse and compare. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of violent video games on children but best combined with another method such as field experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Lucas carried out an experiment with 40 children aged 5-7, observing their play after a cartoon. Table: children in each group (%) | Violent cartoon group | Non-violent cartoon group. Hit the toy at least once | 68% | 33%. Played without hitting the toy | 32% | 67%. (a) Calculate the difference between Hit the toy at least once and Played without hitting the toy for Violent cartoon group and for Non-violent cartoon group, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that media violence causes aggressive behaviour.
items.answer: (a) Violent cartoon group: 36 percentage points; Non-violent cartoon group: 34 percentage points; the difference is larger for Violent cartoon group. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Non-violent cartoon group than for Violent cartoon group among Played without hitting the toy; the figure is lower for Non-violent cartoon group than for Violent cartoon group among Hit the toy at least once; Played without hitting the toy had the highest figure for Non-violent cartoon group. The violent cartoon may have excited children. Qualifications: Hitting a toy is not real violence; artificial setting; short-term effect only; small sample; demand characteristics; ethical concerns. The data also come from laboratory experiments of 40 children in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each difference (36 and 34); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that audiences actively use media to satisfy their own needs?
items.answer: Uses and gratifications model
items.markingKey: Uses and gratifications model: the view that audiences actively use media to satisfy their own needs. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Klapper argued the media mainly reinforce existing attitudes.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain two needs that audiences satisfy through the media, according to the uses and gratifications model.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Selective exposure, perception and retention filter messages. (b) Diversion (escape and entertainment); personal relationships (company, shared topics); personal identity (comparing oneself); surveillance (information about the world).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2] (b) 2 marks for each explained need. [4]

items.stem: Explain two needs that audiences satisfy through the media, according to the uses and gratifications model.
items.answer: Diversion (escape and entertainment); personal relationships (company, shared topics); personal identity (comparing oneself); surveillance (information about the world).
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained need. [4]

items.stem: Mei surveyed 600 young people about why they use social media (more than one answer allowed). Table: young people giving each reason (%) | Aged 13-15 | Aged 16-18. Entertainment and escape | 80% | 73%. Keeping in touch with friends | 84% | 79%. Finding news and information | 28% | 43%. Comparing myself with others | 39% | 44%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Aged 13-15 and Aged 16-18 for Finding news and information (Aged 16-18 minus Aged 13-15)?
items.answer: +15 percentage points
items.markingKey: 43 − 28 = +15 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Interviews with retired people in Bogotá find that they watch daily soap operas because the characters feel like friends and give them something to talk about with neighbours. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: audience needs are shaped by capitalist media and advertising; “choice” takes place within the limits of dominant ideology.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating why people watch reality television. Evaluate the use of official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they give national data on whole populations that no single researcher could collect; positivists see them as objective “social facts” that can be used to test hypotheses. Limitations: they cannot tell us how people feel or why they act as they do; they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why people watch reality television but best combined with another method such as content analysis (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that audiences interpret the same media text in different ways depending on their social position?
items.answer: Reception analysis
items.markingKey: Reception analysis: the view that audiences interpret the same media text in different ways depending on their social position. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Morley found all groups interpreted the Nationwide programme in the same way.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Different groups made dominant, negotiated or oppositional readings.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Explain Philo’s argument that repeated media coverage shapes audiences’ understanding of events, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Philo (Glasgow University Media Group) found audiences could reproduce news-style accounts of strikes and accepted many of their assumptions. Criticism: Some audiences rejected the media account based on personal experience.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Cultural effects theory); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Sipho found this account of a study (Source A) while revising. “A researcher in Lisbon showed a 20-minute news programme about a factory closure to five groups (managers, trade unionists, students, unemployed people and retired people), then held group discussions. Managers mostly agreed with the programme; trade unionists rejected its framing; students accepted parts of it but criticised others.” (a) Explain one limitation of the method used in Source A for studying audience readings of the news. (b) Explain how a neo-Marxist sociologist might interpret the findings in Source A.
items.answer: (a) The detailed data is difficult to compare with other cases. (b) The findings support Hall and Morley: audiences decode the same text through dominant (managers), oppositional (trade unionists) and negotiated (students) readings depending on their social position.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for a relevant limitation; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2] (b) 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the findings in the source. [3]

items.stem: A study in Cape Town finds that people who watch the most television news overestimate the proportion of crimes committed by young people. Explain how a pluralist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Pluralism: audiences are diverse and active, so media cannot impose any single meaning on them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of official statistics for studying how different social groups interpret a TV news report.
items.answer: Strengths: they give national data on whole populations that no single researcher could collect; they are usually free and readily available, saving time and money. Limitations: they cannot tell us how people feel or why they act as they do; interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how different social groups interpret a TV news report but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]
